intervals.label: Hanford run
intervals.locator: Reines Nobel Lecture, section "The Hanford Experiment"; Science 124, 103, first paragraph
intervals.note: Start: Reines says the equipment arrived in the spring of 1953 (A4 season: middle month April, earliest March, latest May); he says they took data "after a few months of operation" and then turned off the equipment. The end is a bound, not a published date: Science (1956) says only that the experiment was "performed at Hanford (1) in 1953".
intervals.quote: Our entourage arrived at Hanford in the spring of 1953.

intervals.label: completed
intervals.locator: Reines Nobel Lecture, section "The Hanford Experiment"
intervals.note: A bound (the year of the experiment), not an end-of-run date. Reines: "After a few months of operation we concluded that we had done all we could in the face of an enormous reactor-independent background. We turned off the equipment and took the train back to Los Alamos."
intervals.quote: A tentative identification of the free neutrino was made in an experiment performed at Hanford (1) in 1953.

name: Cowan–Reines Hanford reactor-neutrino attempt
notes: No collaboration record: a Los Alamos group (Cowan and Reines, with colleagues), not a named collaboration. No detector record is created, as for the Savannah River experiment that followed.

The outcome was a tentative identification, not a detection: Science calls it "a tentative identification of the free neutrino", and Reines writes that "But despite our efforts, background rates due to cosmic rays and electrical noise during reactor off periods frustrated our attempts to achieve the required sensitivity." Back at Los Alamos an underground test showed that the reactor-independent background was in fact from cosmic rays.
The reactor is not named in the sources read ("one of the Hanford Engineering Works reactors"), so the experiment sits on the whole-site point of facility:hanford-site.

physics_goals.locator: Reines Nobel Lecture, letter of 4 October 1952 to Fermi
physics_goals.quote: in the next few months we shall be at Hanford reaching for the slippery particle
physics_goals.value: Detect the free neutrino (antineutrinos from a production reactor) with a large liquid-scintillator detector

summary.plain: In spring 1953 Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines took a liquid-scintillator detector to a plutonium-production reactor at Hanford, Washington, hoping to catch antineutrinos. Cosmic-ray background swamped the signal after a few months, so the result was only tentative; it led them to the cleaner Savannah River experiment.
summary.technical: Delayed-coincidence search for reactor antineutrinos with a 300 L liquid scintillator viewed by 90 two-inch photomultiplier tubes and loaded with cadmium propionate as the neutron capturer, at one of the Hanford Engineering Works reactors; data taken with the reactor on and off. A signal of 0.4 ± 0.2 events/min was seen, but reactor-independent background from cosmic rays prevented the required sensitivity. Predecessor of the 1955-56 Savannah River experiment.
